clinicalPearls: A group of gonadal neoplasms arising from the non-germ-cell supporting tissues (granulosa, theca, Sertoli, and Leydig cells) that are frequently hormonally active

In children an oestrogen-secreting tumour, such as a juvenile granulosa cell tumour, can cause peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious pseudopuberty with breast development and vaginal bleeding
Androgen-secreting variants, such as Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours, can produce virilisation in girls or contribute to precocity in boys
The hormonal effects are autonomous, so gonadotropins are suppressed and the GnRH stimulation test is prepubertal, unlike central precocious puberty
A unilateral adnexal or testicular mass on imaging in a child with signs of sex-steroid excess should raise the suspicion of a hormone-secreting gonadal tumour

Certain sex cord-stromal tumours are associated with genetic syndromes (for example the association of ovarian sex cord tumour with annular tubules and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and Sertoli-Leydig tumours with DICER1 mutations)
Management is primarily surgical, with fertility-sparing resection where feasible, and the histological subtype and stage guide the need for any further therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Sex cord-stromal tumours develop from the steroidogenic and supporting cells of the gonad rather than from germ cells, and they often retain the capacity to synthesise sex steroids. Depending on the cell of origin, they may secrete oestrogens, causing feminising effects and isolated pseudopuberty, or androgens, causing virilisation; some are hormonally silent. Because the hormone production is autonomous and independent of pituitary drive, gonadotropins are suppressed and the changes represent precocious pseudopuberty rather than true, centrally driven puberty. The clinical picture therefore combines the local effects of a gonadal mass with the systemic consequences of the particular hormone being produced, and a subset arises in the context of tumour-predisposition syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty from other causes (e.g. McCune-Albright syndrome, testotoxicosis)
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia or a virilising adrenal tumour
Germ cell tumour of the gonad
additionalInvestigations: Sex-steroid measurement (oestradiol and/or testosterone) with basal LH and FSH (suppressed)
GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test showing a prepubertal, suppressed response
Pelvic or scrotal ultrasound to identify and characterise a gonadal mass
Tumour markers (for example inhibin and anti-Müllerian hormone) that can accompany certain sex cord-stromal tumours
Cross-sectional imaging for staging when a tumour is confirmed
Genetic evaluation for associated syndromes (such as DICER1 or Peutz-Jeghers) where clinically indicated
redFlags: A palpable or radiologically evident gonadal mass with signs of sex-steroid excess
Rapidly progressive virilisation or feminisation suggesting an active tumour
Features of a tumour-predisposition syndrome pointing to hereditary risk
Abdominal pain, distension, or ascites suggesting a large or advanced tumour
Recurrence of hormonal signs after resection, indicating residual or recurrent disease
reference.prognosis: Many sex cord-stromal tumours in children are of low stage and behave in a benign or indolent fashion with an excellent outcome after complete resection, and hormone-driven signs typically regress once the tumour is removed; higher-stage or aggressive histological subtypes carry a less favourable outlook and require additional treatment and surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing precocious puberty to central causes without recognising a hormone-secreting gonadal tumour
Failing to perform a GnRH stimulation test to establish gonadotropin independence
Overlooking an associated genetic syndrome and its implications for the patient and family
Assuming all such tumours are benign and omitting appropriate staging and follow-up
Missing a small contralateral or recurrent lesion after initial surgery
